newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian protesters disrupt Sofia rush hour.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian protesters disrupt Sofia rush hour.

text.p: Opposition supporters blocked rush hour traffic in the Bulgarian capital on Monday morning as protests to demand a general election entered their fifth week.

Sofia public transport went on strike and students blocked main road junctions. In bright morning sunshine, they played football and volleyball on the Eagles Bridge, which is normally choked with early morning traffic.
Many commuters were sympathetic to the disruption. "If walking is what it takes to bring the communists down from power, I'll walk until the end of the year," said a middle-aged housewife.

The ex-communist Socialists are expected to announce a new cabinet later on Monday. The main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) on Sunday declined their last-minute offer of more talks on a coalition, saying they must first hand back their mandate.

Protesters blocked main roads around the country and held strikes in factories and coal mines. In Bulgaria's second city of Plovdiv, public transport stopped work and the UDF mayor appealed to citizens to turn out and join a planned blockade of main roads around the city.

State news agency BTA said a six-day blockade of road and rail links between Bulgaria and Greece had prevented more than 1,000 freight wagons carrying food, coal, liquid fuels and medicine from entering the country.

Miners at the Maritsa-Iztok mines, which supply Bulgaria's thermal power stations, began a strike on Saturday evening, while distribution workers at Neftochim, Bulgaria's largest oil refinery, started one-hour daily stoppages on Thursday.
Several towns have complained of fuel and bread shortages.

Protesters at the town of Doupnitsa, 60 km (35 miles) south of Sofia, kept up their day and night blockade of road and rail links to Greece which began last Wednesday. "People are determined to stay until the Socialists give up," said UDF spokeswoman Vessilka Ousheva in Doupnitsa.
Bulgaria's government has been paralysed since December when Socialist prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned after months of criticism of his handling of the economy.

While the Balkan state has sunk further into crisis, urgent legislation has been left unattended such as voting the 1997 budget and setting up a tough fixed exchange rate regime to restore confidence in the national currency.
Both the European Union and the International Monetary Fund have said that there can be no efforts to help Bulgaria out of crisis until a stable government is in place.

The Socialists have an absolute majority in parliament and barring defections, should be able to win a vote of confidence for their cabinet on Tuesday, but many people fear a repeat of the violence which broke out between police and demonstrators who besieged and ransacked the legislature on January 10.
Dobrev tried on Friday to propose a compromise way out but failed to win the backing of the party leadership.

In an apparently unrelated development, former military prosecutor Colonel Lilko Yotsov and his wife were badly wounded by a bomb which exploded in their car on Monday. Car bombs are frequently used to settle scores in Bulgaria, where the crime rate has soared since the end of communist rule in 1989.
